source_text: Structural members within a roof may be essential for the structural stability of the building and must demonstrate the relevant fire resistance required by paragraph 6.1.
Compartment walls and compartment floors should have the appropriate fire resistance as given in Appendix B, Table B1.
Compartment walls and compartment floors should form a complete barrier to fire between the compartments they separate.
Compartment walls should be constructed as compartment walls where they separate flats from other flats.
Compartment walls should be constructed as compartment walls where they separate flats from common parts.
Compartment walls should be constructed as compartment walls where they separate flats from ancillary accommodation.
Compartment floors should be constructed as compartment floors where they separate flats from other flats.
Compartment floors should be constructed as compartment floors where they separate flats from ancillary accommodation.
A protected shaft is a shaft that enables services, lifts or stairs to pass through compartment floors.
A protected shaft should be enclosed with fire resisting construction.
A protected shaft should achieve the fire resistance given in Appendix B.
A protected shaft should not contain any pipe conveying gas or oil.
Pipes conveying gas or oil may be contained in a protected shaft where the pipe installation meets the relevant provisions for protected shafts.
A protected shaft containing a stair should not contain any services other than electrical wiring for lighting, emergency lighting, fire detection or evacuation lift operation.
A protected shaft containing a lift should be separated from other parts of the building by fire resisting construction.
A protected shaft should be ventilated where necessary to prevent smoke spread.
Openings into protected shafts should be limited to those necessary for their purpose.
Openings in protected shafts should be protected in accordance with the relevant provisions in Section 9.
External walls of flats should meet the relevant provisions for fire resistance where they are required to resist fire spread.
Guidance on cavity barriers in flats is given in paragraphs 6.17 to 6.25.
For the purpose of this document, a cavity is considered to be any concealed space.
To reduce the potential for fire spread, cavity barriers should be provided to divide cavities and close the edges of cavities.
Cavity barriers should not be confused with fire-stopping details.
Cavity barriers should be provided at the edges of cavities, including around openings such as windows, doors and exit or entry points for services.
Cavity barriers should be provided at the junction between an external cavity wall and every compartment floor and compartment wall.
Cavity barriers should be provided at the junction between an internal cavity wall and every compartment floor, compartment wall, or other wall or door assembly forming a fire resisting barrier.
Cavity barriers should be provided in extensive cavities at the maximum dimensions stated in the relevant table.
Maximum dimensions of undivided concealed spaces.
Cavity with surfaces class C-s3, d2 or better: maximum dimension 20m.
Any other cavity: maximum dimension 10m.
It is not appropriate to complete a line of compartment walls by fitting cavity barriers above them.
The compartment wall should be extended to the underside of the floor or roof above.
Cavity barriers, tested from each side separately, should provide a minimum of 30 minutes’ integrity E 30.
Cavity barriers, tested from each side separately, should provide a minimum of 15 minutes’ insulation I 15.
Cavity barriers may be formed by a construction provided for another purpose if it achieves the same performance.
Cavity barriers in a stud wall or partition, or provided around openings, may be formed of steel a minimum of 0.5mm thick.
Cavity barriers in a stud wall or partition, or provided around openings, may be formed of timber a minimum of 38mm thick.
Cavity barriers in a stud wall or partition, or provided around openings, may be formed of polythene-sleeved mineral wool or mineral wool slab under compression when installed in the cavity.
Cavity barriers in a stud wall or partition, or provided around openings, may be formed of calcium silicate, cement-based or gypsum-based boards a minimum of 12mm thick.
These do not necessarily achieve the performance specified in paragraph 6.22.
Cavity barriers provided around openings may be formed by the window or door frame, if the frame is constructed of steel or timber of the minimum thickness in paragraph 6.23(a) or 6.23(b).
Cavity barriers should be tightly fitted to a rigid construction and mechanically fixed in position.
If this is not possible, the junction should be fire-stopped.
Cavity barriers should be fixed so their performance is unlikely to be made ineffective by movement of the building or external envelope.
Cavity barriers should be fixed so their performance is unlikely to be made ineffective by collapse of services penetrating the cavity barriers during a fire.
Cavity barriers should be fixed so their performance is unlikely to be made ineffective by failure of the cavity barrier fixings during a fire.
Cavity barriers should be fixed so their performance is unlikely to be made ineffective by failure during a fire of any material or construction to which cavity barriers abut.
Openings in cavity barriers should be limited to fire doorsets with a minimum E 30 rating, fitted in accordance with Appendix C.
Openings in cavity barriers should be limited to the passage of pipes that follow the provisions in Section 9.
Openings in cavity barriers should be limited to the passage of cables or conduits containing one or more cables.
Openings in cavity barriers should be limited to openings fitted with a suitably mounted and appropriate fire damper.
Openings in cavity barriers should be limited to ducts that are fire resisting minimum E 30.
Openings in cavity barriers should be limited to ducts fitted with a suitably mounted and appropriate fire damper where they pass through the cavity barrier.
For further guidance on openings in cavity barriers see Section 9.
Section 7: Compartmentation.
Compartment walls and compartment floors should be provided where required by this section.
Compartmentation should comply with the provisions in Table 7.1.
Provision of compartment walls and compartment floors.
Wall separating semi-detached houses or terraced houses: compartment wall required.
Wall or floor separating a flat from another flat: compartment wall or compartment floor required.
Wall or floor separating a flat from common parts: compartment wall or compartment floor required.
Wall or floor separating a dwelling from ancillary accommodation: compartment wall or compartment floor required.
A compartment wall should run the full height of the building in a continuous vertical plane.
A compartment wall should be continued through any roof space to the underside of the roof.
A compartment wall should meet the underside of the roof covering or deck, with fire-stopping to maintain the continuity of fire resistance.
A compartment wall should be continued across any eaves.
Junction of compartment wall with roof should follow Diagram 7.1.
Openings in compartment walls and compartment floors should be protected to maintain fire separation.
Openings in compartment walls and compartment floors should comply with Section 9.
A compartment wall or compartment floor should not be penetrated unless the penetration is protected.
Fire-stopping should be provided in accordance with Section 9.
Section 8: Fire resisting construction.
Fire resistance should be determined in accordance with Appendix B.
Elements of structure should achieve fire resistance for the relevant period.
Fire resistance of loadbearing elements should include resistance to collapse.
Fire resistance of separating elements should include integrity and insulation.
The fire resistance performance of doorsets is given in Appendix C.
Fire resisting construction should be continuous at junctions with other construction.
Fire resisting construction should be installed so that its performance is not impaired.
Suspended ceilings contributing to fire resistance should meet the relevant provisions in Appendix B.
Fire protecting suspended ceilings should be supported by construction capable of maintaining support for the required fire resistance period.
Guidance on tests and classifications for fire resistance is given in Appendix B.
Section 9: Protection of openings and fire-stopping.
Openings in fire-separating elements should be limited to those necessary for the function of the building.
Openings in fire-separating elements should be protected to maintain the fire resistance of the element.
Fire-stopping should be used to seal joints between fire-separating elements.
Fire-stopping should be used to seal openings for pipes, ducts, cables and conduits passing through fire-separating elements.
Fire-stopping should be suitable for the fire resistance period required.
Fire-stopping should be securely fixed and remain in position for the required fire resistance period.
Fire-stopping products should be tested in accordance with the relevant standards in Appendix B.
Pipes passing through fire-separating elements should be protected by one of the stated methods.
The pipe should be fitted with a proprietary sealing system that has been shown by test to maintain the fire resistance of the fire-separating element.
The pipe should meet the diameter limits and conditions in the relevant pipe table.
Maximum nominal internal diameter of pipes passing through a compartment wall or compartment floor.
Lead, aluminium, aluminium alloy, fibre-cement or PVC pipes: maximum nominal internal diameter as stated in table.
Any other material: maximum nominal internal diameter as stated in table.
The opening for a pipe should be as small as practicable and fire-stopped around the pipe.
Ventilation ducts passing through fire-separating elements should be protected by fire dampers, fire resisting ductwork, or an alternative tested system.
Fire dampers should be tested in accordance with BS EN 1366-2 and classified in accordance with BS EN 13501-3.
Fire resisting ductwork should be tested in accordance with BS EN 1366-1 and classified in accordance with BS EN 13501-3.
Dampers should be installed in accordance with the manufacturer’s installation instructions and the classification report.
Fire dampers should be accessible for inspection, testing and maintenance.
Doorsets in fire-separating elements should achieve the relevant fire resistance performance given in Appendix C.
Fire doorsets should be fitted with a self-closing device where required by Appendix C.
Fire doorsets should be installed in accordance with the test evidence and manufacturer’s installation instructions.
Glazing in fire doorsets should provide the appropriate level of fire resistance.
Guidance on fire doorsets is given in Appendix C.
Section 10: Concealed spaces.
For the purpose of this section, a concealed space is any cavity within the construction of a building.
Cavity barriers should be provided to restrict the unseen spread of smoke and flame through concealed spaces.
Cavity barriers should be provided in accordance with Table 10.1.
Provision of cavity barriers.
Edges of cavities: cavity barrier required.
Junction between external cavity wall and compartment floor or wall: cavity barrier required.
Junction between internal cavity wall and fire resisting barrier: cavity barrier required.
Cavity barriers should close the edges of cavities around openings.
Cavity barriers should be provided at junctions between cavities and fire-separating elements.
Extensive concealed spaces should be subdivided at the maximum dimensions stated in Table 10.2.
Maximum dimensions of undivided concealed spaces.
Concealed space with surfaces class C-s3, d2 or better: maximum dimension 20m.
Any other concealed space: maximum dimension 10m.
Cavity barriers should achieve the minimum fire resistance stated for integrity and insulation.
Cavity barriers should be installed so they remain effective for the required fire resistance period.
Openings in cavity barriers should be protected.
Further guidance on cavity barriers is given in the relevant earlier sections for dwellinghouses and flats.
The external walls of the building shall adequately resist the spread of fire over the walls and from one building to another having regard to the height, use and position of the building.
The roof of the building shall adequately resist the spread of fire over the roof and from one building to another having regard to the use and position of the building.
Requirement B4 does not apply to material alterations to any prison provided under section 33 of the Prison Act 1952.
candidate_obligation: Exclude Requirement B4 where the work is a material alteration to a prison provided under section 33 of the Prison Act 1952.
candidate_evidence_requirement: Building use record identifying prison status, statutory provision record identifying section 33 of the Prison Act 1952, and works description identifying material alteration scope.

source_text: External walls are constructed so that they resist the spread of fire over the walls and from one building to another.
Roofs are constructed so that they resist the spread of fire over the roof and from one building to another.
Section 11: Resisting fire spread over external walls.
External walls should achieve the relevant fire resistance where the wall is less than the relevant distance from the boundary.
External wall fire resistance should be assessed in accordance with Appendix B and Section 13.
External surfaces of walls should meet the provisions in Table 11.1.
Reaction to fire performance of external surface of walls.
Buildings less than 18m in height: external surface classification as stated in table.
Buildings 18m or more in height: external surface classification as stated in table.
The national classifications do not automatically equate with the equivalent European classifications.
External walls of buildings should meet the provisions for external wall materials and attachments where applicable.
Regulation 7 applies to materials and workmanship.

Building work shall be carried out with adequate and proper materials which are appropriate for the circumstances in which they are used, are adequately mixed or prepared, and are applied, used or fixed so as adequately to perform the functions for which they are designed.
Building work shall be carried out in a workmanlike manner.
Building work shall be carried out so that relevant metal composite material does not become part of an external wall, or specified attachment, of any building.
candidate_obligation: Ensure relevant metal composite material does not become part of an external wall or specified attachment of any building.
candidate_evidence_requirement: External wall and specified attachment material schedule identifying all installed materials and confirming no relevant metal composite material is included.

source_text: Subject to paragraph (3), building work shall be carried out so that materials which become part of an external wall, or specified attachment, of a relevant building are of European Classification A2-s1, d0 or A1.
candidate_obligation: For a relevant building, ensure materials that become part of an external wall or specified attachment are European Classification A2-s1, d0 or A1 unless exempt under paragraph (3).
candidate_evidence_requirement: External wall and specified attachment material schedule, classification reports for each material showing A2-s1, d0 or A1, and exemption schedule identifying any paragraph (3) exemption.

source_text: Paragraph (2) does not apply to the listed materials.
Cavity trays when used between two leaves of masonry.
Any part of a roof other than any part of a roof which falls within paragraph (iv) of regulation 2(6).
Door frames and doors.
Electrical installations.
Insulation and water proofing materials used below ground level.
Intumescent and fire-stopping materials where the inclusion of the materials is necessary to meet the requirements of Part B.
Membranes.
Seals, gaskets, fixings, sealants and backer rods.
Thermal break materials where the inclusion of the materials is necessary to meet the thermal bridging requirements of Part L.
Window frames and glass.
Relevant building means a building with a storey at least 18 metres above ground level and which contains one or more dwellings, an institution or a room for residential purposes.

In a building with a storey 18m or more above ground level, insulation products, filler materials and other materials used in the external wall construction should achieve the required classification.
For buildings described in regulation 7(4), materials should meet regulation 7(2).
External wall systems may be assessed using a full-scale test method where applicable.
External wall systems may be assessed against BR 135 using data from BS 8414 tests.
The external wall construction should not contribute to fire spread.
Cavity barriers should be provided in external wall cavities where required by the cavity barrier provisions.
Cavity barriers in external walls should be provided in accordance with Sections 5, 6 and 10 as applicable.
Section 12: Roof coverings.
The designation of roof coverings should be in accordance with Table 12.1 and Table 12.2.
Roof covering classification should be determined in accordance with BS EN 13501-5.
Limitations on roof coverings.
Roof covering designation BROOF(t4): unrestricted distance from relevant boundary.
Roof covering designation CROOF(t4): minimum distance from relevant boundary as stated in table.
Roof covering designation DROOF(t4): minimum distance from relevant boundary as stated in table.
Roof covering designation EROOF(t4) or FROOF(t4): minimum distance from relevant boundary as stated in table.
Separation distances are measured to the relevant boundary.
Limitations on plastic rooflights.
TP(a) rooflight: limitations as stated in table.
TP(b) rooflight: limitations as stated in table.
Class D-s3, d2 plastic rooflight: limitations as stated in table.
Plastic rooflights should also meet the internal lining provisions where applicable.
Rooflights should be separated from each other and from relevant boundaries in accordance with the table limitations.
The roof covering should not promote fire spread from one building to another.
Guidance on roofs forming part of a means of escape is given in the means of escape sections.
Section 13: Space separation.
The amount of unprotected area in the side of a building should be restricted to reduce the risk of fire spread to adjacent buildings.
A relevant boundary is the boundary used for determining space separation.
An unprotected area is any part of the external wall that has less fire resistance than required.
The permissible unprotected area should be determined using the relevant method or table.
Methods for calculating unprotected area are given in Appendix B.
External walls within 1m of the relevant boundary should achieve fire resistance from both sides.
External walls 1m or more from the relevant boundary should achieve fire resistance from the inside.
Relevant boundary rules should be applied using the diagrams in this section.
Relevant boundary.
Boundary distance measured at right angles to the wall.
A notional boundary should be assumed between buildings on the same site where required for space separation.
Notional boundary.
A notional boundary is treated as a relevant boundary for the purposes of calculating space separation.
Unprotected areas may be calculated using the simple approach where the building meets the relevant limits.
Permitted unprotected areas for small residential buildings.
Minimum distance to relevant boundary and maximum total unprotected area as stated in table.
Where the simple approach is not applicable, the enclosing rectangle method may be used.
Enclosing rectangle method.
Calculations should be made on a conservative basis where exact information is not available.
